Measuring the AI readiness of the geosciences: a solid-earth perspective

Technical report, 30 October 2026. Analysis package geoscience-ai-readiness, branch main; source, data and notebooks at github.com/gaia-hazlab/geoscience-ai-readiness. Contact: Marine Denolle, University of Washington.

Goal. Measure the AI readiness of the geosciences, from a solid-earth perspective. We treat readiness as three measurable things: how often research papers use machine learning (ML), how much of the data a community holds exists in ML-ready form, and how visible that data is on the platforms where ML practitioners look. Solid earth here means seismology, distributed acoustic sensing (DAS), geodesy, radar deformation and the simulations that model them.

Summary

  • Method uptake is not the bottleneck. Earth and environmental science articles mention ML at least as often as the average field: 5.1% against 3.9% in 2025. Geophysics sits at 4.8% for 2023 to 2025.
  • Solid-earth simulation communities adopt ML surrogates more slowly. Per 100 articles naming a numerical method, geophysics has 5.3 ML-surrogate articles and earth-surface processes 1.9, against 13.5 in atmospheric science and 32 in physics.
  • The readiness gap is volume. ML-ready benchmarks hold 0.27% of the EarthScope seismic archive (at most), 0.08% of the Sentinel-1 SAR archive, and none of the GNSS archive. Reanalysis is the exception: 20% of ERA5 exists in an analysis-ready cloud format.
  • Simulation output is the largest untapped solid-earth resource. All public solid-earth ML-ready simulation corpora total 2.48 TB; one CyberShake study kept 75 TB and handled 2.5 PB during its run. ML-ready corpora in other physics and atmospheric science total 101 TB.
  • DAS adoption. Among abstracts whose analysis uses DAS, the share using AI as a method rose from 15.3% in 2020 to 28.6% in 2025 (unvalidated abstract-level screen); 198 of 249 such papers use deep learning and 3 a foundation model.
  • The AI-ready label is rare everywhere. 707 of 78,241,222 DataCite datasets use it. Geoscience datasets are not underrepresented on Hugging Face by repository count (3,990 against 4,624 biomedical, name matching).
  • Complexity favors AI and also limits it. Native data are large (12,000 DAS channels on one array) while measured effective dimensions of climate fields are tens (18.5 to 90), close to image benchmarks. Minimal coupled models need 1 to 17 balance equations, so the unknowns sit in closures. Heavy tails are untested or unresolved: 4 of 13 tested fits favor a pure power law. Outcome labels are thin: EM-DAT lacks total damage for 41.5% of natural-hazard events.

1. Do geoscientists use ML?

The geosciences are not behind in reaching for ML. The question for readiness is whether the data and simulations that solid-earth science holds can feed those methods at scale.

2. A solid-earth case: DAS

The DAS topic frame holds every OpenAlex article or review whose title or abstract matches "distributed acoustic sensing", 2020 to 2025. Claude Opus 5.5 labeled each abstract under a fixed codebook; the labels are screening evidence, not actual use, and have not yet been validated against human coding.

In the core seismology journals the AI-as-method share of DAS papers is 10 to 19%, below the frame average, because much of that literature establishes the instrument (response, coupling, imaging). Whether DAS adopts AI more slowly than its journals as a whole needs a non-DAS baseline from the same journals; that run is sized (about 8,400 articles) but not done.

A benchmark is a designed subsample, so a small share is not by itself a deficit. It bounds what can be trained, and in particular pretrained, without new curation. Reanalysis shows what full packaging looks like; it is also the discipline where ML models now train on the full record, though this analysis does not test causation.

4. Simulations and surrogate models

The observational comparison misses the half of solid-earth science that runs on simulations: wavefield and Green's-function databases, dynamic rupture, ground-motion hazard and full-waveform inversion. Two measures capture it: how often simulation communities publish ML surrogates, and how much simulation output exists in ML-ready form.

Across Earth and environmental sciences the index rose from 0.45 in 2016 to 10.9 in 2025, ahead of all fields (7.2). The growth is carried by climate and atmospheric science; geophysics and earth-surface processes trail.

5. Datasets on platforms

The AI-ready label is young: DataCite datasets using it number 5 in 2020, 27 in 2023 and 156 in 2025. Platform counts do not show a geoscience lag; the gap sits in the volume packaged, not in the label or the hub.

6. Why the geosciences are hard, and why that suits AI

Complexity is measured along four axes, each with its own units, and the axes are never added into one score. Every value below comes from the sourced tables in docs/complexity_2026-10-30/, where each row carries a source, an as-of date, a quote and a flag saying whether the number was read in the source text.

AxisWhat the tables showWhy it suits AIWork that remainsAI evidence rows
DimensionalityNative data are large: 12,000 channels on one DAS array, 47,354 seismic stations in one study. Published effective dimensions of climate fields are 18.5 to 90; image benchmarks give 7 to 43 (MLE).Learning cost scales with intrinsic, not nominal, dimension; large data over modest structure is where learned representations outperform hand-built features.No published effective dimension for seismogram archives, DAS or ERA5; one DAS study finds near-uniform singular values.8 successes, 2 limitations
Coupled physicsMinimal coupled models need 1 to 17 scalar balance equations; Navier-Stokes, Maxwell and magnetohydrodynamics need 4 to 8.The laws are few and known; the uncertainty sits in empirical closures (friction, permeability, rheology), which hybrid models can learn while keeping the balance laws.Learned closures fail out of distribution (+4 K warming in two climate studies); no sourced learned friction or rheology closure was found.5 successes, 3 limitations
Heavy tails24 geoscience power-law rows report an exponent; 13 were tested against alternatives and 4 favored a pure power law.Learned models can pool events across regions and catalogs, beyond what a single parametric fit uses.AI forecasts degrade on record-breaking extremes; magnitude estimates saturate near M5.5 to 6.0; tail-aware evaluation is missing.1 success, 3 limitations

The profile reads as a work plan. Seismology and weather and climate are each measured on four of five columns, and they miss different things: seismology has no effective dimension for its archive, and weather and climate has only qualitative evidence on unobserved drivers. DAS and radar have sourced AI successes but no sourced limitation; geodesy was not assessed for AI results. None of the three has tail tests or unobserved-driver numbers in these tables. Cells marked not assessed were not searched and say nothing about the discipline.

All paper counts are keyword co-occurrence in titles and abstracts and never establish actual use. The semantic screen labels the abstract only; a missing abstract or a failed answer stays unclear, never negative. Benchmarks are paired only with the archive they were drawn from.

9. Limitations

  • Keyword co-occurrence measures attention, not use. OpenAlex field labels are content-based and move AI-heavy papers into Computer Science.
  • The DAS screen is unvalidated; a 130-abstract blind validation sample is drawn and awaits two coders.
  • Archive volumes mix definitions and dates (2020 to 2026). No cumulative volume is published for DAS experiments, USGS NWIS, CyberShake, Syngine or EQSIM.
  • Hugging Face counts match repository names and are upper bounds.
  • Small packaged shares bound what can be trained without curation; they do not show that more packaging is needed for every task.
  • The complexity and AI-evidence tables are purposive samples of the literature, not a census; successes and limitations were both sought, but their counts do not measure how often AI succeeds.
  • Equation counts depend on the source and dimensionality chosen; they measure model size, not difficulty.
